en: Kedārabhaṭṭa: *Vṛttaratnākara*,
with Sulhaṇa’s *Sukavihṛdayānandinī* commentary.
The First Chapter. Homage to Sarasvatī!
[He who is] endowed with glory, joined with splendor, and illuminated by the beautiful Gaṅgā.
Adorned with various faces, graced by the elevation of the crescent moon as its crest-ornament,
endowed with noble qualities, and always worshipped with garlands by all the attendant hosts—
victory to the body of the Lord, which is like the science of prosody, and is venerated by the three worlds. 1.
In ancient times, there was born in the lineage of Kṛṣṇātreyas a preeminent southern scholar named Velāditya; his son was the brilliant poet Bhāsa;
and his son, named Sulhaṇa, [composed] this work called the Vṛttaratnākara, consisting of verses with most graceful words—
He composed a treatise on prosody named *Sukavihṛdayānandinī*.
At the beginning of the treatise, the author, preceded by a salutation to his chosen and presiding deity, states the connection and purpose of the work in three verses:
"Having bowed to Brahmā, who is worshipped by Acyuta, for the sake of attaining a continuous flow of happiness..."
To Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, who is accompanied by Gaurī and Vināyaka.
There was a preeminent twice-born man named Pavyeka, who was a knower of the meaning of the Vedas and the Śaiva scriptures;
he had a son named Kedāra, who was devoted to the worship of Śiva’s feet.
Therefore, this *Chandaḥ* [treatise], endowed with the characteristics of the *lakṣa* system,
is composed under the name *Vṛttaratnākara* for the easy understanding of beginners.
The meanings of the Vedas are *vedārthāḥ*.

Those scriptures (*śāstrāṇi*) which have Śiva as their deity are *śaivāni*. He who knows both those meanings of the Vedas and the Śaiva scriptures is so described. There was a most excellent twice-born man named Pavyeka; of that Pavyeka, there was one named Kedāra, who was devoted to the worship of the feet of Śiva.
There is a son;
by him this meter, whose characteristics will be described, is composed.

It is "endowed with both definition and illustration" (*lakṣalakṣaṇasaṃyutam*): the illustration (*lakṣya*) is the example, while the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) consists of the arrangement of fixed syllables, morae, and gaṇas; it is endowed with both of these.
What is its name?
It is named *Vṛttaratnākara*. "Meters" (*vṛttāni*) refers to those beginning with the *śrī*; they themselves are the "jewels" (*ratnāni*), and their "mine" (*ākara*) is the place of their origin.
For what purpose? For the sake of the accomplishment of happiness;
"accomplishment of happiness" means success through happiness, and it is for that sake, for the accomplishment of happiness.
Of whom?
Of the foolish, those of dull intellect.
Having done what?
Having bowed down; to whom? To Śaṅkara, the Great God (Mahādeva).
Of what nature is he?
He is the "benefactor of the world" (lokaśaṃkara), because he brings about (karoti) welfare (śaṃ), that is, happiness, for the worlds; thus, he is the benefactor of the world.
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
Worshipped by Brahmā and Acyuta, and honored by Viriñci and Nārāyaṇa;
furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is accompanied by Gaurī and Vināyaka—that is, joined with those two, Gaurī and Vināyaka.
For what purpose?
For the sake of accomplishing happiness and lineage.

"Happiness" consists of the nature of the bliss of the supreme Brahman; "lineage" refers to sons, grandsons, and so forth; the "accomplishment" of these two is their attainment—for that purpose, for the sake of accomplishing happiness and lineage.
The connection is that [he] "having bowed" and "having prostrated.
This is a *viśeṣaka* consisting of three verses. (1–3)
He explains what is meant by the word *chandas*:
"That which was taught by teachers such as Piṅgala as worldly [prosody] is twofold, distinguished by *mātrā* and *varṇa*; that is what is described here as *chandas*. (KVrk 1.4)
This very thing is called *chandas* in the treatise (*śāstra*),
which has been stated and expressed by teachers such as Piṅgala who are practitioners of the science of prosody;
it is worldly (*laukika*), existing in the world, and not Vedic.
Because it is of no use in poetry and the like; [it is] "twofold," meaning of two kinds. To the question "How so? he says: "by the distinction of *mātrās* and syllables."

By the distinction of *mātrās*, [there is] the *āryā* and so forth; by the distinction of syllables (*varṇa*), [there is] the *śrī* and so forth; and by the distinction of meters (*vṛtta*), [there is the same]. // 4 //
Now he states the number of verses: "The measure of this *Chandas* [text], which is composed of six chapters, should also be clearly known as one hundred and thirty-six."

Those which are studied are called *adhyāyas*, and they possess the characteristics that will be described hereafter. These consist of the six types of meters defined by the six suffixes: *saṃjñā*, *abhidhāna*, *mātra*, *vṛtta*, *samavṛtta*, *ardhasamavṛtta*, and *viṣamavṛtta*.
This is to be understood as the measure—the total number—of the treatise on prosody (*chandaḥśāstra*) composed in six chapters, which is one hundred and thirty-six. // 5 //
Now he states the enumeration:
"By these ten syllables—my, ra, sta, ja, bha, na, ga, la, and anta—the entirety of speech is pervaded, just as the three worlds are pervaded by Viṣṇu. (KVrk 1.6)
The traditional teaching (*āmnāya*) is that by the mere mention of the first syllable, "ga," both the words *guru* (heavy) and *laghu* (light) are understood.
By these ten syllables— ma, ya, ra, sa, ta, ja, bha, na, la, and ga— ...
The entire Śabdabrahman is also pervaded;
like what?
Like the three worlds.
By whom?
By Nārāyaṇa, who has reached the state of existence. // 6 //
He states the definition for each of these:
"The all-heavy (sarvaguru) consists of *m*; those with *l* at the end (*la-anta*) and *ya-ra* at the end (*ya-ra-anta*) consist of *ga* and *la*;
those with *g* in the middle (*g-madhyā*) consist of *y* and *b*; and *j*, *b*, and *n* consist of three *la*s. Thus, there are eight groups (*gaṇas*) of three syllables here. (KVrk 1.7)
In this treatise on prosody (*chandaḥśāstra*), that which has all heavy syllables (*guru*) is the *magaṇa* (sarvaguru), for example: ( _ _ _ ).

The *yagaṇa* and *ragaṇa* are those whose first and last syllables are light (*laghu*). "Light at the beginning and end" (*mukhāntarlau*) means the first and the end; "inside" (*antaḥ*) means the middle. Those two whose first and middle syllables are light are the *yagaṇa* and *ragaṇa*: ( ^ _ _, _ ^ _ ).
The *sagaṇa* and *tagaṇa* have light syllables at the end (*antagalau*).

At the end, that is, at the conclusion, those two which have a heavy (guru) and a light (laghu) syllable are the sagaṇa and tagaṇa, as follows: (^^_, __^). Those two which have a heavy syllable in the middle and at the beginning are the jagaṇa and bhagaṇa, as follows: (^_^, _^^).

*Tri-la-naḥ*: three light [syllables], namely the *nagaṇa* (as in ^ ^ ^). These—*ma*, *ya*, *ra*, *sa*, *ta*, *ja*, *bha*, and *na*—are the eight *gaṇas*; the meaning is that they are the *gaṇas* of the *varṇavṛtta* meter.

Because the rules for the groups of morae (mātrāgaṇa) will be prescribed in the sūtra to be stated [later], he states a restriction out of concern that even those [groups] beginning with "four heavy" (caturguru) might be designated as "groups" (gaṇa) and so forth.
"Trikāḥ" means those whose measure is three; thus they are called "trikāḥ. // 7 //
Now he speaks of the groups of morae (*mātrāgaṇa*):
"In this context, the four-mora groups are to be known as having a heavy syllable at the end, in the middle, or at the beginning;
these groups, consisting of four light syllables with one added [heavy], are established in the *āryā* and other meters. (KVrk 1.8)
In the mātrāvṛtta meters beginning with the Āryā, five groups (gaṇas) of four morae each are to be understood.
How so?

"Those whose heavy syllables are at every beginning, middle, and end": all of them have their heavy syllables at the beginning, middle, and end; thus, those whose heavy syllables are at every beginning, middle, and end are called "those whose heavy syllables are at every beginning, middle, and end."
They should be understood as being accompanied by and joined with four light syllables. // 8 //
In order to distinguish between heavy and light syllables, he says:

"That which is accompanied by an anusvāra, ends in a visarga, is long, or is followed by a conjunct consonant—whether it occurs at the end of a quarter-verse (pāda) or not—is to be known as *g-vakra* (curved); any other is *mātṛka-lṛju* (straight). (KVrk 1.9)
That which occurs together with an *anusvāra* is "with *anusvāra*" (*sānusvāra*).
That which ends in a *visarga* is "with *visarga*" (*savisarga*).
A long vowel has two morae (*dvimātra*).
One who is intent on conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is intent on a *yukta* [consonant cluster];
by the word "and" (*ca*), that which ends in a consonant (*vyañjana*) is also included.

A quarter (*pāda*)—which consists of a measured number of syllables, is composed of metrical feet (*gaṇa*), and possesses the characteristics to be described hereafter—is the fourth part of a verse; a short vowel (*laghu*) occurring at the end of such a quarter may optionally (*vibhāṣā*) be considered long (*guru*).
And this [the *yati*] should be understood to occur at the end of only the second and fourth quarters according to the poetic convention (*kavisamaya*). For example:
"Generally, the intellects of those whose defeat is imminent become most utterly perverted;
nevertheless, Rāma lusted after the deer, even though a being made of gold was impossible. Thus it is said.
And so it is said:
"The Lord of Śrī, the abode of the world, entered the house of Vasudeva in order to govern the glorious world," and other such passages should be consulted.
And having established that [consonant] as curved (vakra) in the grid (prastāra), he states the definition of the light (laghu):
"The other, the *mātṛka*, is to be known as straight (*ṛju*).
A phoneme (*varṇa*) consisting of a single measure (*ekamātra*), which is devoid of the *anusvāra* and so forth, is light.
And that [line] on the grid is straight and even. // 9 //
Regarding the heaviness [of a syllable] established by the rule "and those followed by a conjunct" (yuktaparaś ca), he states an exception:

"In this system, a conjunction of phonemes at the beginning of a word is designated as *krama*. By virtue of that [consonant] standing before [the vowel], even a heavy syllable may sometimes become light. (KVrk 1.10)

A word (*pada*) is that which ends in a case-suffix (*vibhakti*). The conjunction (*saṃyoga*) of the phoneme (*varṇa*) occurring at the beginning of that word is to be understood here in this treatise as having the technical designation "conjunction" (*krama*).
By means of that preceding *krama*, there shall be lightness (*laghutā*) for a phoneme situated at the end of the prior word, even if it has attained the status of being heavy (*guru*).
In some cases, it is in accordance with the *lakṣa* (the defining characteristics).

Now, what indeed is this so-called "order" (*krama*)? It is said to be conjunction (*saṃyoga*). This is the convention adopted by the ancient masters, such as Piṅgalanāga and others, as well as by poets such as Kālidāsa and others.
Conjunction is sequential conjunction. // 10 //
In that regard, as for [the rule] by means of conjunction (*grasa-saṃyoga*),
this is its illustration:
"Young mustard greens, fresh rice, and thick curds."
O beautiful one, with little expense, the common folk eat sweet food.
As an example of a compound with a short vowel:
"By your modesty, my own modesty was carried away; even in the abode of the moon, it was stolen and not retained. O beloved, where will that dense darkness of bees and sheep-herds go again? Thus.
One who lacks wealth incurs shame; overcome by shame, one’s splendor fades away.
Deprived of splendor, one is humiliated; through humiliation, one falls into despondency.
Despondent, one succumbs to grief; overwhelmed by sorrow, one falls away from right understanding.
Alas, the lack of wisdom leads to ruin; indeed, death is the abode of all calamities.

"They were stolen by me alone; for instance: 'Out of affection for their homes, the city women—regardless of the strain on their waists caused by the weight of their thick, lofty breasts—ran swiftly as they were being carried away, their upper garments slipping down and producing delight in the eyes of the fickle-eyed [onlookers]. Thus it is said.
As it is said in the Bodhapradīpa:
"By those whose every step has adorned this earth with sacrifices, and by whom this circle of the world was conquered and given as a gift to the twice-born..."
Even those kings, repeatedly assuming the manner of bubbles upon the mass of foam in this lake of existence, have swiftly gone to their dissolution.
As in the *Śiśupālavadha*:

"Having quickly reached the immersion in the lake of the navel, it set out for the seizing of the garment. As an example with the conjunction *bh*: [as in the verse beginning] "Having quickly reached... and so forth.
O moon-faced one, this bee, having abandoned the blossoms of the creeper, desires to drink from your face, mistaking it for a lotus.
And so it is said:
"It wanders in the forest of female bees that has been released," and so forth;
[it wanders] among the flowers of the excellent trees, in the lotuses of the celestial Gaṅgā, upon the temples of the elephants of the gods, and in the tresses of the celestial women.
O bee, this is a delusion that brings you pleasure while standing, lying down, or waking; it is for this reason that you wander in vain among the *ketaka* flowers.
Why is it stated "at the beginning of a word"?
So that it does not apply elsewhere;
for example, as in the case of *grasaṃyogena*.
"What do you gain by looking at what is incomplete? Look, O fair-thighed one, without hesitation!
For water sipped with the tip of a blade of kusha grass never causes thirst to vanish, even after a very long time.
Thus is the example with a short *saṃyoga*.
"They both placed their feet upon the earth.
And likewise:
"There, the King of Vatsa carried off the beloved daughter of Pradyota."
For example, by means of a *bhrasaṃyoga*:
"O supreme hero of the Aras, have your glories, white as jasmine, not made everything bright?
For even today, the lotus-faces of your enemies' wives still bear a dark hue. And so forth.
What is meant by "in some cases"? Let it not apply everywhere,
as in the case of the conjunction *grasaṃyoga*.
"By the blow of his foot, the earth suddenly falls into a state of peril;
the very step of Viṣṇu is one where the seizing grip of the planets is shattered by his whirling, mace-like arms."
As for the combination with *bhra*, it is as in:
"There the six-sensed one indeed wanders in vain. Some consider this to occur at the beginning of a quarter-verse (*pāda*).
That is inconsistent,
because there is no connection between the sūtra and the example cited.
Nevertheless:
"Young mustard greens, fresh rice, and thick curds—
O beautiful one, with little expense the country folk eat what is sweet. Thus was the example demonstrated by the noble lady.
In the Āryā meter, there is no fixed arrangement of feet.

By defining the characteristic of the Āryā as "the first half and the second half" through the mention of the "first half" and "second half," the author himself makes it known that, for the time being, there is no fixed arrangement of feet in the Āryā; this is also evident from the reading of the *Piṅgala-sūtra*.
"Vowels [are followed by] half-morae, and a consonant [is followed by] half a mora. Therefore, the reading "at the beginning of a word" (*padādau*) is superior; enough with this digression. // 11 //
Now he states the technical names:
"The names for [the numbers] four, five, six, six, and so forth should be known from common usage.
A 'pāda' is to be known as a fourth part; 'yati' is designated as a pause. (KVrk 1.12)
Namely: the four Vedas;
the five arrow-fingers (five sense faculties);
and the six seasons.
There are seven musical notes and sages;
eight Vasus;
nine cavities of the body.
The ten directions;
the eleven Rudras;
the twelve Ādityas.
The Viśvedevas are thirteen;
the worlds are fourteen;
the lunar days (tithis) are fifteen, and so forth.
He states the definition of a *pāda*: "The *pāda* is to be known as a fourth part.
A portion consisting of a fourth part of a *vṛtta* whose characteristics are to be described hereafter shall be designated by the term *pāda*.
Now he speaks of the pause (yati):

the pause is known as a "severance" (viccheda). This pause, beginning with the cessation [of recitation], has been handed down through the lineage of teachers; it should be applied to syllables that are divided by words within the middle of a line.
For the followers of Sāṃkhya connect the words "ocean" and so forth with the word "ascetic" (*yati*).
This is the meaning that remains.
Regarding this, the teachers say:
"There is a pause (yati) everywhere at the end of a quarter-verse, especially at the end of a half-verse,
and at the end of words such as 'samudra' and others, whether their case-endings are manifest or unmanifest."
In some cases, however, a pause may occur even in the middle of a word, as in the case of *samudra* and similar terms,
provided that the preceding and following parts do not consist of a single syllable each.
In the case of a sandhi, the vowel should sometimes be regarded as belonging to the preceding part, and sometimes as belonging to the following part;
this is to be observed when considering the *yati*, provided that the substituted element (*ādeśa*) is treated as belonging to the following part.

"Particles such as *ca* and others that are invariably connected with the preceding word are treated like the final element of that preceding word; and particles such as *pra* and others that are invariably connected with the following word are treated like the initial element of that following word."
The caesura (*yati*) occurs everywhere at the end of a quarter-verse (*pāda*),
as for example:
"The two cheeks of Śrī’s [face], which bring about the highest good, possess a luster equal to the full moon."
Just as in such passages as, "Where the musk serves as an ornament for the reflection of Hari," and likewise,
"Obeisance to that Great God, the wearer of the crescent moon."
But this is especially so in the case of a half-verse (*ślokārdha*);
for example:
"Without service to the king, our merit has become fruitless."
It was like an invaluable ornament for the women of the inner apartments. Thus [it is said].
In the word *agādityam*, there is no sandhi with the vowel *a* of the word *antaḥpureṇa* because of the final consonant;
this does not occur even in a compound, as for example in:
*surāsuraśiroratnasphuraccaraṇamañjarī*.
We pay homage to Śiva, whose pair of lotus-feet has been turned golden.
At the end of the words beginning with "samudra" (ocean), there is the distinction between the manifest and the unmanifest;
that is, the distinction of the manifest, meaning the distinction of the clearly evident.
In cases where the case-ending is unmanifested or where it is manifested within a compound,
there are examples of these two as follows:
"The Yakṣa performed [his rites] in the waters made holy by the bathing of Janaka’s daughter."

The term *vyaktāvyaktavibhaktikaḥ* (distinguishing the manifest and the unmanifest) is connected everywhere with the rule *yatiḥ sarvatra pādāntaḥ* (the pause occurs at the end of every quarter-verse). I bow to Him who has made the world and time His garment, whose throat is black, the Great Time (*Mahākāla*), whose only remaining digit is the crescent moon, and who is the crest-jewel upon the moon.
Moreover:
Homage to Śambhu, who is beautiful with the chowrie of the moon kissing his lofty head, and who is the foundation pillar for the construction of the city of the three worlds.
In some cases, however, a pause may even occur in the middle of a word, such as in the word "samudra" and others,
provided that the preceding and following parts do not consist of a single syllable each.
For example:
"It is not enough that the shore of the heated golden bracelet is embraced by the opposite [cool] direction.
Why [is it said] "in the ocean and so forth"? [To exclude cases such as: "The heated golden bracelet... etc.
Let there be no elision of a vowel at the end of a word when it occurs in the middle of a *pada*. For example:

"praṇamata bhavabandhakleśanāśāya nārāyaṇacaraṇasarojadvandvamānandahetuḥ" (Bow down to the pair of lotus-feet of Nārāyaṇa, which is the cause of bliss for the destruction of the afflictions that bind one to worldly existence).
However, if the preceding and following portions consist of only one syllable each, a pause (*yati*) within the middle of a word is considered faulty. For example:
*etasyāṃ gaṇḍatalamamalaṃ gāhave candrakakṣāmiti* and *etāsāṃ rājati sumanasāṃ dāmakaṇṭhāvalambīti*.

"This hip of the lotus-eyed one produces distress for me"—in this [example], the vowel at the junction (*saṃdhi*) sometimes behaves like the end of the preceding element and sometimes like the beginning of the following element.

This is the meaning: whatever single sound is prescribed at the junction of two vowels, that sometimes becomes like the end of the preceding element and sometimes like the beginning of the following element.
As in the previous example:
"It might be delightful at a place other than the confluence of the Yamunā;
likewise, [the mountain] bears a thick cloud of vermilion dust arising from the frontal globes of the elephants of Indra."
The treatment as if [the preceding element] were the first of the following (parādivadbhāva) is, for example,
in my own *Vyāyoga*:
"Those whose mouths were suddenly torn open by their own enemies became split apart in battle."

"Fortunate is he who, seated in a celestial chariot, beholds one fighting with his own body— his left side like a sword-sheath and his right side like a blade, one side struck by the blow and the other providing the counter-blow. And so forth.
If the substitute is treated as if it were part of the subsequent element,
for example: *saptarṣihastāvacitāvaśeṣeṣv adho*...
"Vivasvān," and so on; by the word "etcetera" (ādi), [examples such as] "vitataghanatuṣāraḥ kṣodaśubhrāṃśuvartma svavirale" and others are included.
Particles such as *ca* and so forth, when always connected with a preceding word, are treated like the final part of that preceding word.
The meaning is that a pause (yati) should not be made before them. For example:
"svāduḥsvacchaṃdasalilamidaṃ prītaye kasya na syāt" (To whom would this sweet, pure, and limpid water not be a source of joy?).
Furthermore, particles such as *pra* and others, when invariably connected with a subsequent word, are treated as if they were the beginning of that subsequent word.

The meaning is that one should not entertain thoughts directed toward them as being superior. For example, everything such as "the unbearable separation from him casts sorrow into my heart" and so forth should be inferred. // 12 //
The wise declare that even and uneven positions are respectively even and uneven. (KVrk 1.13)
The first, third, and so forth positions are *ayuk*, meaning uneven; the second, fourth, and so forth positions are *yuksama*, meaning even.
Now, he states the divisions of meters:
"Even, half-even, and likewise the other, uneven meter. (KVrk 1.13)
Regarding the phrase "it occurs in the Veda":
*vṛtta* (meter), which will have its characteristics explained below, is of three kinds:
even (*sama*), half-even (*ardhasama*), and uneven (*viṣama*).

In that regard, *sama* (even) is so called because all its constituent parts (*avayava*) are equal, such as the *śrī* meter and others; *ardhasama* (half-even) includes the *upacitrā* and others; and *viṣama* (irregular) includes the *padacaturūrdhva* and others.
He states the definition for each of these:
"That [meter] whose four feet are characterized by identical metrical definitions..."
Those who know the truth of the science of prosody declare that to be a "sama-vṛtta" (even meter).
That meter whose four quarters all possess identical characteristics is called "even" (sama) by those who know prosody.
Now, he describes the "half-even" (ardhasama).
If the third foot of a verse is equal to the first,
and the second is like the fourth, that meter is called *ardhasama* (half-equal).
That *vṛtta* whose first and third quarters possess identical characteristics,
and whose second and fourth quarters likewise do so,
is called *ardhasama* (half-equal).

He states the definition of the irregular (viṣama) meter: "Those experts in the science of prosody say that when the characteristic mark differs from one to another even within a single four-line stanza, that is called an irregular meter."
The teachers say that when a meter has a different, mutually distinct characteristic in all four quarters, it is called *viṣama* (irregular).
Now, he states the rule for the quarters of meters,
beginning from a quarter consisting of one syllable and increasing by one syllable at a time.
The *pṛthakchanda* meter occurs with feet ranging up to twenty-six syllables.
From a single-syllable quarter-verse, by increasing one syllable at a time for each quarter-verse, there arise the meters (*chandas*).
How far does this extend? Up to the *utkṛti* consisting of twenty-six syllables.
Beyond that, the *caṇḍavṛṣṭi* and others are proclaimed as the *daṇḍaka* meters.
Above the *utkṛti* class consisting of twenty-six syllables, there are the *daṇḍaka* meters beginning with *caṇḍavṛṣṭi*.
The word "the rest" refers to this section;
that [rest] is to be understood from other treatises.
For fear of excessive length, Kedāra has not stated [the rest] here;
the remainder is characterized by three gāthās and six pādas. (KVrk 1.18)
The remainder—three-footed and six-footed verses following the section on *jāti*—are *gāthās*.
Now, he states the *jātis* of the meters:
*uktā*, *atyuktā*, likewise *madhyā*, *pratiṣṭhā*, and another preceded by *supratiṣṭhā*.
The Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, and Paṅkti; KVrk_1.19 //
The *triṣṭubh* and the *jagatī* are likewise considered, as well as the *atijagatī*;
the *śarkarī* is preceded by *ati*, and from that [point], the *aṣṭi* and *aty-aṣṭi* are recorded.
Dhṛti, Atidhṛti, Kṛti, Prakṛti, Ākṛti,
Vikṛti, Saṅkṛti, as well as Abhikṛti and Utkṛti.
Having thus stated the names of the meters, I shall now describe in due order the characteristics of all metrical feet, beginning with those measured by syllabic instants (mātrāvṛtta).
The one-syllable [meter] is called *ukta*; the two-syllable, *atyukta*;
and the three-syllable, *madhyā*.
The four-syllabled is *pratiṣṭhā*;
the five-syllabled is *supratiṣṭhā*;
the six-syllabled is *gāyatrī*.
The *uṣṇih* has seven syllables;
the *anuṣṭubh* has eight syllables;
the *bṛhatī* has nine syllables.

The pause (*yati*) occurs at the sixth and sixteenth [syllables]. In it, various young women gather at the crossroads.
O best of kings, in the cities of your foremost enemies— which were once delightful with songs— there now prevails, by the prowess of your arm, the playful gait of wild bulls and elephants.
The Vāṇinī meter always consists of the gaṇas na, ja, bha, ja, ra, accompanied by a *ga*.
That meter in which there are the gaṇas *nagaṇa*, *jagaṇa*, *bhagaṇa*, *jagaṇa*, and *ragaṇa*, followed by two *gurus*, is called *vāṇinī*. For example:
"The deer-eyed woman, whose heavy hips were bound with a girdle, whose arrows were awakened by the sound of the small bells (*kiṃkiṇī*) attached to its strings—"
O friend, this eloquent woman, skilled in clever speech, produces great joy; when seen, she takes hold of the mind. 95.
The *śikhariṇī* consists of eight syllables, with caesuras at the sixth and eleventh syllables; it has the *na*, *sa*, *bha*, *la*, and *ga* gaṇas.
That meter in which there is a *yagaṇa*, *magaṇa*, *nagaṇa*, *sagaṇa*, *bhagaṇa*, followed by a short (*laghu*) and a long (*guru*) syllable, is called *śikhariṇī*.
There is a pause (*yati*) after the sixth and eleventh syllables.
She has a face like the moon and eyes that rival the petals of a blooming blue lotus.
Moving gracefully with a gait languid from the weight of her heavy hips,
this courtesan, whose breasts are like lofty peaks of fatness, stirs agitation even in the hearts of sages with her sidelong glances. (96)
The *pṛthvī* [meter] consists of the gaṇas ja, sa, ja, sa, ya, la, with eight syllables per foot and a heavy syllable (guru) at the end.
That meter in which there is a *jagaṇa*, a *sagaṇa*, a *jagaṇa*, a *sagaṇa*, a *yagaṇa*, a short syllable (*laghu*), and a long syllable (*guru*) is named *pṛthvī*. For example:
"O lady with beautiful hair, why is this mass of your hair unadorned? And why, O lady of the earth, is your waist devoid of a fine girdle?"
Therefore come, adorn yourself and cast aside your anger; for in this spring festival, O fair-limbed one, youth will pass away in just five or six days.
The *diṅmuni* meter consists of the sequence of syllables *vaṃśapatrapatita*, defined by the ganas *bha-ra-na-bha-na-la-ga*.
That meter in which there is a *bhagaṇa*, a *ragaṇa*, a *nagaṇa*, a *bhagaṇa*, a *nagaṇa*, a short syllable (*laghu*), and a long syllable (*guru*) is called *vaṃśapatrapatita*.
The pause (*yati*) occurs after the tenth and seventh syllables. For example:
"Those whose minds are afflicted by thirst do not know [this] at all in the city of your enemy..."

O King, even the water in the ponds of the palace was covered by a mass of fallen leaves from trees— blown there by the wind— even though the deer were close by; for when the heat was great, they sought shelter beneath the eaves.
When the sequence consists of ra, sa, ma, ra, sa, la, and two ga-ga, it is then called Hariṇī.
That meter in which there is a *nagaṇa* and a *sagaṇa*, followed by a *magaṇa* and a *ragaṇa*, and then a *sagaṇa* with a short (*laghu*) and a long (*guru*) syllable, is called *hariṇī*.
The pause (*yati*) occurs after the sixth and fourth syllables. For example:
*vadanam amalaṃ dhatte śobhāṃ śaśāṅkasamāśritām* (The face bears a stainless beauty resting upon the moon).

The pair of her ears performs the swaying sport of the god of love; a vast and exceedingly pure necklace gleams upon the surface of her breasts— if this were not so, surely the deer-eyed woman’s heart would have been stolen away by him.
Some say it is the life of Ṛṣabha. // 99 //
The Mandākrāntā metre consists of fourteen syllables per quarter, with the sequence ma-bha-na-ta-ta-ga-ga.
That metre in which a quarter-verse consists of a magaṇa, a bhagaṇa, a nagaṇa, two tagaṇas, and two gurus (long syllables) is called Mandākrāntā;
it has a caesura after the fourth and sixth syllables. For example:
*mandākrāntādharakisalayā pāṇipadmaṃ dhunānā*.
With her slender body trembling,

her face perspiring, her skin bristling with horripilation, and her eyes slightly closed, the newlywed bride, loosened by the passion of a deep embrace, brings intense delight to the heart of the groom.
If the feet consist of the gaṇas na, ja, bha, ja, ja, la, and a guru, it is the Narkuṭaka meter.
A *nagaṇa*, a *jagaṇa*, two *gaṇas* consisting of a *jagaṇa* and a *gaṇa*, two *jagaṇas*, and a short and a long syllable—this meter is called *narkuṭaka*;
others call it *avitatha*. For example:
"In the arrival of the spring breeze, which causes grief to people separated from their lovers..."

this skill of mine in speaking truthfully has become fruitless.
Declare the *kokilaka* as having four *yatis* at the seventh, fourth, and seventh syllables.

"O friend, it is certain that here at home, that weak woman herself must be suffering intensely day and night, afflicted by the heavy fever of love. (102)
In the *dhṛti* meter, there are twelve, six, and seven syllables; the *kusumitalatāvellitā* consists of the ganas *ma*, *ta*, *na*, and *ya*, followed by two *ya*s.
That metre in which there is a *magaṇa*, a *tagaṇa*, a *nagaṇa*, and three *yagaṇas* is called *kusumitalatāvellitā*.
The pause (*yati*) occurs after the fifth, sixth, and seventh syllables. For example:
"The abundance of fragrance from the dwelling [of bees] as they shake the clusters of garden lotuses..."

In *atidhṛti*,
with six, six, seven, and five syllables, and the *ma*, *na*, *sa*, and *ra* gaṇas followed by a heavy syllable (*guru*), there is the *meghavisphūrjitam* metre.
That meter in whose quarter there are the *yagaṇa*, *magaṇa*, *nagaṇa*, and *sagaṇa*, followed by two *ragaṇas* and a long syllable (*guru*), is named *meghavisphūrjita*.
The pause (*yati*) occurs after every six and seven syllables. For example:
*samāyātaḥ svairaṃ kuṭajakusumāmodavāhī samīraḥ* (The breeze, carrying the fragrance of *kuṭaja* flowers, has arrived at its own will.)

The Śārdūlavikrīḍita meter consists of twelve syllables, with the sequence ma-sa-ja-sa-ta, followed by a heavy syllable (guru).
That meter in which a quarter-verse consists of a *magaṇa*, a *sagaṇa*, a *jagaṇa*, a *sagaṇa*, two *tagaṇas*, and a long syllable (*guru*) is named *śārdūlavikrīḍita*.
The pause (*yati*) occurs after the twelfth and seventh syllables. For example:
*śrīkhaṇḍācalakaṃdarātsarabhasaṃ nirgatya sāṃdraṃ drumāṃ-*
Thus, repeatedly and sportively brandishing his bow with its beautiful mass of swaying campaka filaments,
this spring breeze shall, by means of his *śārdūlavikrīḍita* (tiger’s play),
forcibly slay the elephant of pride even among women who are fierce with indignation.
In the *Kṛti* meter, the *Suvadanā* is known to consist of seven, seven, six, and six syllables, with the sequence *ma-ra-bha-na-ya*, followed by *bha-la-ga*.
That meter in which each quarter-verse consists of a *magaṇa*, *ragaṇa*, *bhagaṇa*, *nagaṇa*, *yagaṇa*, *bhagaṇa*, a short syllable (*laghu*), and a long syllable (*guru*) is called *suvadanā*.
There is a pause (*yati*) after every seven syllables, and the sixth syllable is also a pause. [An example:
"She whose thighs resemble plantain stalks, who has large, heavy breasts, and whose eyes are like those of a deer."
Slender-waisted, with a beautiful line of hair, possessing pure and even teeth and a moon-like face,
this fair-faced young woman— skilled in clever speech— reveals her inner state through her side-long glances as if they were her own, and instantly intoxicates the hearts of the youths. 106.
If there are three *ra* syllables and two *ga*s here, by such a characteristic, it is the name of a meter (*vṛtta*).

That meter in whose foot there are three *ragaṇas* (three short syllables followed by one long), a *jagaṇa* (one short syllable followed by two longs), and a long and a short syllable is called by the name *vṛtta*; that is to say, it is designated as such.

Pride arising from the attainment of prosperity occurs only occasionally in the mind of a mountain [or a steadfast man], even though he is skilled in the science of logic (*pramāṇavidyā*) for shattering the web of objects of knowledge belonging to others.
Nor has he ever tasted the pleasure of touching another's wife, whether she be beautiful or plain;
such is his conduct that it is borne upon the heads of men, and therefore it must be reflected upon.
In the *prakṛti* [meter],
this *sragdharā* is proclaimed as consisting of three *mra*, *bha*, and *na* gaṇas, joined with the triple pause of the three sages (*trimuni*).
That meter in which a quarter-verse consists of a *magaṇa*, a *ragaṇa*, a *bhagaṇa*, a *nagaṇa*, and three *yagaṇas* is called *sragdharā*.
There is a pause (*yati*) after every seven syllables, occurring three times [in each quarter].
[It describes her] whose face has the luster of a blossoming lotus, who is stainless, and whose eyes are wide and expanded.
With their girdles shimmering and their great jewels sparkling,
spreading the beauty of their rounded hips,
the regions of their resplendent navels bring delight to the hearts of men.
Walking along the royal road, the king’s wives wore garlands of blooming *vikaṅkata* flowers. // 108 //

In the *ākṛti* meter, there are two *bha*s, *na*, *ra*, *na*, and *ra*, followed by a heavy syllable (*guru*), with a pause at the tenth, twelfth, and seventeenth syllables; this is indeed the *madraka*.
That meter in which the feet consist of a *bhagaṇa*, a *ragaṇa*, and a *nagaṇa*, followed by a *ragaṇa*, a *nagaṇa*, a *ragaṇa*, a *nagaṇa*, and a heavy syllable (*guru*), is called *madraka*.
The pause (*yati*) occurs after the tenth and twelfth syllables. For example:
"How can I, by means of these false words spoken by you, provoke his incomparable anger?"

O friend, I have never heard nor seen anything unpleasant from him; how is it that this beloved makes my heart full of passion with his words, even as he now rolls about intensely upon the pair of my feet, having cast off the net of his feet? 109.
If, in this modification,
there are *na*, *ja*, *bha*, *ja*, *bha*, *ja*, *la*, and *ga*, then it is the *Aśvalalita* meter, consisting of twenty-seven syllables.

That meter in which each quarter-verse consists of a *nagaṇa*, a *jagaṇa*, a *bhagaṇa*, a *jagaṇa*, a *bhagaṇa*, a *jagaṇa*, a *bhagaṇa*, a short syllable (*laghu*), and a long syllable (*guru*) is called *Aśvalalita*.
The pause (*yati*) occurs after the eleventh and twelfth syllables. For example:
*samaravinirjitārinivahakṣitīśvaravicitramaśvalalitam* (The horse-play of the various lords of the earth, who have utterly conquered the hosts of enemies in battle).

Beholding this which bestows a marvel upon the heart, poets say of you: "Surely the Lord of the Gods (Indra) has accepted this excellent horse of the King; otherwise, he would not be seen here in the sky with such an abundance of horses. (110)
In the *mattākrīḍa* meter, there are the ganas ma, ta, na, na, la, and a *guru* (g); it consists of eight, five, ten, and four syllabic instants respectively.
That meter in which a quarter-verse consists of two *magaṇas*, a *tagaṇa*, a *nagaṇa*, two *nagaṇas*, and a *laghu* (short) and *guru* (long) syllable is named *Mattākrīḍa*.
The pauses (*yati*) occur after the eighth, fifth, and tenth syllables. For example:
*dṛṣṭvā cāndraṃ bimbaṃ rātrau karanikaravinihitatimiranikaram* (Having seen the lunar orb at night, with its mass of rays having dispelled the mass of darkness...)

O ornament of the earth, in that city of yours, which is now filled with flowers in full bloom during the springtime, the citizens sing at their own will; there, the herds of deer— freed from the fear and trembling of worldly existence— are intoxicated by unrestrained sporting.

If in the *saṃkṛti* meter there is the sequence *bhūta-muni-nairyati* (seven, seven, five, and four syllables), and then *sbhau bhanayāḥ* (sagaṇa, bhagaṇa, bhagaṇa, nagaṇa, and two yagaṇas), it becomes the *tanvī* metre.
That meter in which a quarter-verse consists of a *bhagaṇa*, a *tagaṇa*, a *nagaṇa*, a *sagaṇa*, two *bhagaṇas*, a *nagaṇa*, and a *yagaṇa* is named *tanvī*.
Its caesura occurs after five, seven, and twelve syllables. For example:
"She whose lotus-face is like the moon, with beautiful, tremulous eyes, and exceedingly lovely..."

O fair-browed one, this slender-limbed young woman, with her full hips, heavy pair of breasts, and her rounded, delicate arms and hands, dwells in my heart like the very abode of the shark-bannered god who conquered the three worlds; she produces in me no small amount of joy here. 112.
In the *atikṛti* meter, there are *krauñcapada* feet consisting of *bha*, *ma*, *sa*, *bha*, *na*, *na*, *na*, and *guru*; here, the caesura occurs after five, five, six, and seven syllables.
That meter in which a quarter-verse consists of four *gaṇas*—namely *bhagaṇa*, *magaṇa*, *sagaṇa*, and *bhagaṇa*—followed by four *nagaṇas* and a heavy syllable (*guru*), is called *Krauñcapadā*.
The caesura occurs after the fifth, eighth, and seventh syllables respectively. For example:
*Krauñcapadā yā romaśagātrī vikaṭadaśanatanuratiparuṣatanuḥ* (The one who is *Krauñcapadā* has hairy limbs, deformed teeth, and an exceedingly harsh body).
She who casts sidelong glances, possesses slender hips, and has a pair of uneven breasts with a mass of tawny hair;

she who, laughing in private, sheds tears from her eyes while turning away from her own husband—O friend, abandon her if you desire what is most beloved, and enjoy the pleasures of the senses here for a long time. 113.
In the *utkṛti* meter,
the *bhujaṃgavijṛmbhita* consists of eight *vasus* (eight), two *īśas* (eleven), and a *chada* (seventeen), followed by the sequence *ma-ma-ta-na-yuga-na-ra-sa-la-ga*.
That meter in which a quarter-verse consists of two *magana*s, one *tagaṇa*, three *nagaṇa*s, a *ragaṇa*, a *sagaṇa*, and a short and long syllable (*laghu-guru*) is named *bhujaṅgavijṛmbhita*.
The pause (*yati*) occurs at the eighth, eleventh, and seventh syllables. For example:
*prāleyāṃśujyotsnākāntadyutiśubham avimalasadvitānamanohare*...
When, in a pleasure-chamber radiant with the pure luster of swarms of bees drawn by the fragrance of blooming flowers,

even a woman of noble family assumes the conduct of a courtesan through an overflow of passion during the festival of love, and when even her lover, as if out of sheer joy, reveals his true nature in private, then it is not the mere unfolding of a serpent's coils.
If it consists of six *mo*s, a *nā*, and *ṣaṭ* (six) *saga*s, and is joined with nine, six, five, and seven *ya*- and *ti*-feet, it is called *apavāha*.
That meter in which there is a *magaṇa* at the beginning of each quarter, followed by six *nagaṇas*, two *sagaṇas*, and two *gurus*, is called *apavāha*.
The pauses (*yati*) occur after the ninth, sixth, sixth, and fifth syllables respectively. For example:
*ātmānaṃ kalayati tṛṇamiva suragurudharaṇitalasuragavāmartho...* (The wealth of the gods on the surface of the earth, [which is like] the preceptor of the gods, regards itself as a blade of grass...)

The world beholds with contempt that man who, though he constantly offers pure wealth from his ever-blossoming lotus-face to supplicants here— his generosity mocking the vast riches of Kubera— is now seen as a mere outcast, his body emaciated and his intellect and wisdom dissolved by various calamities. (115)

Setting aside the remaining *jāti* and other categories, he states the *daṇḍaka* meters according to their definitions, beginning with: "All of that is known as *daṇḍakas*.
"If there is no *yagaṇa* here, and then seven *repha*s (r-gaṇas), then it would be the *caṇḍavṛṣṭiprayāta* *daṇḍaka*. (KVrk 3.116)
In this treatise, there is a *daṇḍaka* meter named *Caṇḍavṛṣṭiprayāta*.
It occurs when there are two *nagaṇas* followed by seven *ragaṇas*.
Many names have been given to it by the two sages Śatamāṇḍava and Ṛṣi; for example:

"O traveler, why do you exert yourself in vain?

For example, *arṇa* consists of eight *ragaṇas*:
"The breeze, fragrant with the scent of jasmine, quickly removes the sweat born of passion and exertion from amorous women."

The row of trees on the bank of the Madhupa river, adorned with shimmering sprouts, produces for the prince here a manual of amorous graces; for he, the son of the king, who brings joy to the eyes of the beautiful women of Bhujagapura— eyes that have never known the blow of a thunderbolt from a rival suitor— displays his radiant playfulness before his beloveds like a treasury of nectar.

Like an ocean with nine *ragaṇas*, it shines forth with waves rising higher than lofty mounds of foam, white as masses of froth, possessing the splendor of the high peaks of the three-eyed mountain; it is filled with sea-monsters,
whales, and timingilas, and its beauty is attained upon its vast expanse, signaling the courtyard of the sky.
O beloved, may this ocean— the foremost among those dwelling in the waters, the abode of the God of Gods who reclines upon the serpent-couch, and the very glory of whose mansions is known to all—
come within the range of your vision and bestow great joy, serving as a source of diversion with its punnāga and pūga trees growing upon its shores.
Just as a serpent is provoked by ten strokes,

so does this spring season provoke the woman separated from her lover; it is a season that brings joy through the intense longing increased by contact with the long sighs of women parted from their lovers, and which carries the fragrance of blossoming *bakula*, *karṇikāra*, mango, *unnāga*, *mākanda*, *kaṅkelli*, and fine *campaka* trees, while the Malaya breeze blows.

O friend, worship the pair of feet of Him who is beloved by women with bowed limbs; He is the one desired by those longing for a flood of joy, the deer-eyed ones who are distressed by the mountain [of worldly existence].
O young woman, what is gained by this burning pride of yours, which always destroys the happiness of women and is as flickering as the tip of a tongue of blazing flame?

By means of those eleven clouds, she who was separated from her beloved and whose life was on the verge of destruction was restored; for that banner of bees—the entire swarm intoxicated by the wine of *kadamba* flowers shaken by the wind skilled in destruction—was present.
She beheld the sky adorned with a garland of lightning like a celestial river, a row of dark blue clouds frequented by flocks of cranes, which bestowed joy upon the eyes.
He beheld a delightful flock of cātakas, their sweet voices raised in song, intoxicated with passion and longing for the future satisfaction of rain; meanwhile,
he himself repeatedly spread his magnificent plumage.
The beloved woman, enchanting the god of love, dances, generating delight with the beauty of her graceful movements of the feet.
Just as the Creator of Play [the Buddha] was awakened by twelve [verses], so too,

if one has attained awakening through the sound of the beautiful songs of female cuckoos whose throats are purified by tasting fresh, new sprouts, in a forest on the Cakravāla mountain range; and if that forest is filled with the beauty of the woods, its branches heavy with the weight of excellent blossoms from many flowering *pāṭala*, *karṇikāra*, mango, *siṃduvāra*, and noble *aśoka* trees, with its tender shoots swaying— [then one attains awakening].
This spring breeze, the sole kinsman of the God of Love, which brings about the graceful dance of the shoots of the *mādhavī* vines and possesses a prideful grasp of the clouds,

repeatedly desires to cause the trembling of the edges of the curls of women— curls clinging with drops of sweat born from the fatigue of love-play— as if manifesting the world-conquering command of Smara.
Unrestrained by thirteen *ragaṇas*, it is as follows:

She bears a lotus-face resembling the moon; her high breasts are adorned with a magnificent necklace and a lower lip like a ripe bimba fruit; her heart and navel are reached by the line of fine body hair;

and the surface of the earth is agitated by her eyes dancing upon the lap of the stage of her lower limbs, which are illuminated by the luster of gems attached to golden circular earrings set upon her pair of ears.

Adorned with a girdle jingling with small bells that produce a sweet sound, her pair of thighs is shapely and tapering, following the curve of her rounded hips; she wears tinkling anklets upon her two lotus-red feet.

As she moves gracefully, she utterly agitates even the hearts of sages who have no other refuge—she who, with the tips of her shimmering garment fluttering, awakens the goddess of Love and brings the entire world under her sway.

It was adorned like a conch shell with fourteen jewels; in some places by spreading canopies of *taracca* and *caṃdavallī* creepers, in some places by clusters of tree-vines, in some places by moving circles of crocodiles, and in some places by *pūga* trees growing from waterless soil.
In other places, it was graced by beautiful groves of betel vines together with rows of *ghanasā*, mango, *hiṃtāla*, and *tāla* palms.
In some places, you caused the earth to tremble with the tumultuous roar of leaping serpents;
in other places, you were drenched by water-carrying breezes that had attained the perfection of fragrance through contact with the scent of the blooming, swaying fresh *campaka* flowers.

Having seen the ocean—the source of many jewels and a treasury of joy—whose waters were carried away, scattered, and swept clean by the wind, and having reached its boundary marked by the bridge, you swiftly brought to fulfillment the gaze of the eyes that fell upon it.

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), there are daṇḍakas such as the *samudra* consisting of fifteen *ra*s and the *bhujaṅga* consisting of sixteen *ra*s; thus, they are known by names created according to one's desire. // 117 //
That which is known by the names *pracitaka* and *samabhidha*, and is considered a *daṇḍaka* by those of steadfast intellect, consists of two *na*s followed by seven *ya*s.
After two *nagaṇas*, a *daṇḍaka* named *pracitaka* is recorded as consisting of seven *yagaṇas*.

As before, here too, by the process of increasing the number of *repha*s (the syllable 'ra') in each successive quarter-verse (*caraṇa*), the *daṇḍakas* are formed through the increase of all the *gaṇas* beginning with *yagaṇa*. Just as the increase of meters was previously described as an increase of one syllable at a time, so too is there an increase characterized by three *repha*s; and this should be understood according to the traditional instruction of the teachers for as long as it reaches one syllable short of a thousand.
They exist.

Although it has been stated by some that *daṇḍaka* meters extend up to a thousand syllables, nevertheless, through the increase of triplets (*tṛka*), they amount to exactly one less than a thousand. // 118 //
