The Fourth Chapter:
The Chapter on Half-Equal Meters. Now he speaks the chapter on half-equal meters.
If there is *sa*, *la*, and *ga* in the odd quarters,
and *bha*, *ya*, *bha*, *ga*, and *ru* in the even quarters, it is the *upacitra* meter.
Although one should have said "in this quarter," the author of the Sūtra has stated "half" with reference to the half [verse] in this chapter on *ardhasamavṛtta* meters; thus there is no fault.

When there are three *sagaṇas*, a light syllable (*laghu*), and a heavy syllable (*guru*) in the odd quarters—the first and the third—and when there are three *bhagaṇas* and two heavy syllables in the even quarters—the second and the fourth—then the *ardhasamavṛtta* named *upacitrā* occurs.
For example: [Example omitted as per instructions]
In the city of your enemy, the earth appeared as if it were stripped of its great serpent-skin;
seeing this strange sight by day, the female deer did not enter their dwellings out of fear.
If the first three feet contain the *ojas* (odd) gaṇas and the even feet have *na*, *ja*, and *ja* followed by *ya*, it is *drutamadhyā*.

In that *ardhasamavṛtta* where, in the odd (first and third) quarters, there are three *bhagaṇas* followed by two *gurus*, and in the even (second and fourth) quarters, there are a *nagaṇa*, a *jagaṇa*, a *jagaṇa*, and a *yagaṇa*, that metre is named *drutamadhyā*. For example:
*dṛṣṭivilāsaviśeṣamaśeṣaṃ vividhagatīravacoracanāṃ ca* //
Youth itself, having bestowed discernment by the god of love, swiftly instructs the young bride.
If there is a guru in both the even and odd pādas, it is Sayugāt;
if there is a bhagaṇa and two gurus in the even pāda, it is Vegavatī.

When there are three *sagaṇas* and a heavy syllable (*guru*) in the odd quarters, and in the even [quarters] there are three *bha-gaṇas*, two *na-gaṇas*, and two heavy syllables, it is then called *Vegavatī*. For example:
"O friend, this woman with high and full hips, afflicted by love, goes sportively to the dwelling of a certain lover who is the sole treasure-house of good deeds. (3)
If there is a guru at the odd positions and the second and fourth, and if there are *ma*, *sa*, *ja*, and *ga* at the even positions, it is *Bhadravirāj*. 4.4.

If in the odd feet—the first and third—there occurs a *jagaṇa* and a *ragaṇa* following a *tagaṇa*, and if there is a long syllable (*guru*), and if in the even feet—the second and fourth—there occur a *magaṇa*, a *sagaṇa*, and a *jagaṇa*, followed by a long syllable, that meter is named *Bhadravirāṭ*. For example:
"O King, [this world] is bound by one as bright as the jasmine flower and the moon, who dwells within the interior of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*)."
These glories of yours, which are pure, auspicious, and all-pervading, have been brought to the twilight upon the mountain of Hara for the sake of the waters.
In the *asama* meter, there is a *sagaṇa*, a *jagaṇa*, and two *gurus*; in the *samā* meter, it is *bha-ra-na-ga-ga*.

When the odd feet (first and third) consist of a *sagaṇa*, a *jagaṇa*, a *sagaṇa*, and a long syllable (*guru*), and the even feet (second and fourth) consist of a *bhagaṇa*, a *ragaṇa*, a *nagaṇa*, and two long syllables, that metre is named *Ketumatī*. For example:
"O King, by you who have entered the field of battle with nothing but your flashing sword as your companion, the enemy army—endowed with horses and elephants—has been conquered. (5)
The Ākhyānikī metre consists of the ganas ta, ja, ga, ru, ga; and if there is a ja, ga, ru, ja, ga, ru, followed by a guru (long syllable), it is [the same].

In the odd (first and third) quarters, there are two *tagaṇas*, a *jagaṇa*, and a heavy syllable (*guru*); in the even (second and fourth) quarters, there are a *jagaṇa*, a *tagaṇa*, another *jagaṇa*, and two heavy syllables. That meter is named *ākhyānikī*. For example:

"O Lord of Avanti, those kings who were your enemies, whom you encountered, have been slain along with the entire host of their adversaries; thus has your fame, which traverses the intermediate space, become an *ākhyānikī*. (6)

In the Jatau meter, there are *ja*, *ta*, and *ga* gaṇas; in the odd positions, there is a *go* (four short syllables), and in the even positions, there should be *ta*, *ta*, *ja*, and *ga*. This is the Viparītapūrvā.

That metre in which the first and third quarters consist of a *jagaṇa*, a *tagaṇa*, a *jagaṇa*, and two *gurus*, while the even quarters consist of two *tagaṇas*, a *jagaṇa*, and two *gurus*, is named *viparītākhyānikī*. For example:
"Surely the Lord of my life will come together, having heard my words full of supreme compassion;
otherwise, by the power of fate, another *ākhyānikī* with its [feet] reversed would occur here for me."
The *ākhyānikī* is called the "news-bearer.

Although both of these are included within the previously mentioned *upajātī*, they are recited in the chapter on "Half-Even Meters" (*ardhasamavṛtta*) for the sake of their specific technical names. // 7 //
In the *hariṇaplutā* meter, there is a light syllable after the first two [syllables], a heavy syllable in the odd positions, and in the even positions, the sequence is *na*, *bha*, *ra*, and *bha*.

That metre in which there are three *gaṇas* consisting of three light syllables (*sagaṇa*) in the odd feet, and in the even feet there are a *na-gaṇa*, a *bha-gaṇa*, a *bha-gaṇa*, and a *ra-gaṇa*, is called *hariṇaplutā*. For example:
If a traveler on the road moves with swift gait like a leaping deer across very uneven paths, then at the arrival of the clouds, he meets his beloved in the form of half her body [the lightning]. (8)

In the *aparavaktra* meter, there is a heavy syllable (*guru*) after the sixth syllable in both halves; then, in the odd pādas, there is a *na*, *ra*, *la*, and *ra*, while in the even pādas, there is a *na*, *ja*, *ma*, *ra*, *ja*, and *ra*.

In the odd pāda, there are two *nagaṇas*, a *ragaṇa*, a short syllable (*laghu*), and a long syllable (*guru*); in the even pāda, there are a *nagaṇa* and a *jagaṇa*, followed by a *jagaṇa* and a *ragaṇa*. That metre is named *aparavaktra*. For example: May that right [face] of the enemy of Madana, whose eyes are as tawny as a water-calf and which is adorned with the crescent moon—[the face] that causes fear to others but is not frightening to the virtuous—remove all fears.
Although this [meter] is included within the *vaitālīya* category, it is presented here for the sake of its specific designation. // 9 //
When there is no *yuga* (ya) following *na*, *yu* (ya), and *repha* (ra), and when *na*, *ja*, *ja*, and *ra-ga* occur in the even [pādas], it is *puṣpitāgrā*.

That meter in which there is a *nagaṇa* (two shorts) in the odd quarter, a *yagaṇa* (one long and two shorts) following a *ragaṇa* (three shorts) in the even quarter, and in the even quarters a *nagaṇa*, *jagaṇa*, *jagaṇa*, *ragaṇa*, and a heavy syllable (*guru*), is called *puṣpitāgrā*.

O moon-faced friend, the branch of the *aśoka* tree, possessing trembling new shoots, has its tips blossomed merely by the touch of your foot; therefore, abandon your pride toward him. This great festival of Love is passing away into emptiness.
This [verse] is also stated here as an *aupacchandasika* for the purpose of indicating its specific technical name. // 10 //
The wise call this *vaitālīya* by the name *aparavaktra*;
some likewise designate it as *puṣpitāgrā* or *aupacchaṃdasika*.
In the odd [pādas], there may be ra-ja-ra-ja; but in the even [pādas], ja-ra-ja-ra followed by a guru constitutes this meter, known as Matī from the yava.

The meaning is that when the odd *pādas* contain a *ragaṇa* and a *jagaṇa*, and the even *pādas* contain a *jagaṇa* and a *ragaṇa*, followed by a *guru* (long syllable), that *vṛtta* is called *yavātparāmatī*. For example:

"O Lord of the Mālava land, having conquered your enemies along with their entire armies by force, you have forcibly brought under your control the whole earth, which is abundant with rice, mung beans, barley, and wheat. (12)
Thus ends the fourth chapter, on the Half-Equal Meters, in the *Vṛttaratnākara-chaṃdovṛtti* titled *Sukavihṛdayānaṃdinī*, composed by Sulhaṇa.
Chapter Five:
The Chapter on Unequal Meters.
The chapter on uneven meters (*viṣamavṛtta*) begins.
The "mouth-foot" (*mukhapāda*) consists of eight syllables.
[Section on *Padacaturūrdhva* (5.1–5)]
When the others [the gaṇas] increase successively by one mātrā each from this [first],
and it constantly possesses a beauty produced by its various feet, that is called by those of pure intellect the metre named *padacaturūrdhva*. 5.1.
The first quarter consists of eight syllables,
while the subsequent second, third,
and fourth quarters increase— meaning they are augmented— by four syllables each, starting from that first quarter.
What is the meaning of "in sequence"?
The second consists of twelve syllables;
the third consists of sixteen syllables.
The fourth [meter] consists of twenty syllables; thus they have attained an increase in sequence.
Because it attains beauty through various and diverse feet arranged in twenty-four ways, constantly and without interruption, that *vṛtta* has been named *padacaturūrdhva* by the teachers.
For example:
O Lord of the Earth, it has been heard that those enemies whom you, having stepped forward and drawn your bow, struck down upon the field of battle with your arrows, suddenly departed from life.
Those who follow the four-footed path do not waver; they fall right there, pierced by the arrow.
In this case, because there is no "gaṇa-pāda" (group-foot), heavy and light syllables are not required.
Furthermore, when expanded here, it becomes twenty-fourfold:
sixteen, twelve, eight; sixteen, twenty, twelve, eight, and so forth. // 1 //
In this [meter], which possesses a first *mudita* rhythm and is endowed with uneven feet, a heavy (*guru*) syllable pair occurs at the end, marked here by the prefix *āṅ*.
In this [verse], there occurs a *pīḍa* meter characterized by a sequence of beautiful, well-distributed syllables.

In this meter, which possesses uneven feet— consisting of eight, twelve, sixteen, and twenty syllables respectively, composed within the *padacaturūrdhva* where the first foot follows the *udita* rule—
the term *āpīḍa* occurs when a *pīḍa* (a specific metrical arrangement) is joined with the prefix *ā*. The meaning is "an *āpīḍa*."
Under what condition? He says:
when there is a pair of heavy syllables at the end (*nidhana*). That is, when that [meter] has two heavy syllables at its conclusion (*avasāna*).
Of what kind is it? He says:
That [meter] is so described because it has a pause or stop (*yati-virāma*) resulting from the expansion of feet that possess sustained brilliance.
Since two heavy syllables (*guru*) are prescribed at the end, we consider that Kedāra permits the remaining syllables here to be light. For example:
*dhruvamiha vanitānām*...
When the breeze from the Malaya mountains— the friend of Love— begins to blow, for women dwelling in separation whose hearts are fixed upon the virtues of their beloveds,
the destruction of their lives inevitably occurs.
In the Vedic tradition (*chandas*), because three heavy syllables do not occur in the *āpīḍa* meter, it is not called by the name *chargaṇḍa*.
This [meter] also consists of twenty-four permutations (*prastāra*), as before.
Having extracted nine from those twenty-four, he speaks in order to designate them as equal: // 2 //
In this world, the mark first rests upon one foot,
and then the fourth mark, produced by the other foot, likewise appears.
The pair of feet is unaltered, while the other part here is a bud. 5.3.
The first [foot] of the Āpīḍa, namely the fourth foot arising from the other [set], takes to—that is, resorts to—the characteristic marked by twelve syllables, which is the second quarter (pāda).
What is the meaning?
There are twelve syllables in the first quarter.

The second [foot] consists of eight syllables; furthermore, another pair of feet is characterized by being unaltered and lacking secondary suffixes—this is what is called *kalikā*. Although it should be called *mañjarī*, it is referred to as *kalikā* for fear of breaking the meter; since they have the same meaning, there is no fault. For example:
In this Kali age, when the wicked are friends and the virtuous are met with hostility,
and when the moon has suddenly become turbid, [the world] is in a state of agitation.
Thereafter, dwelling here produces joy in the minds of those who are free from pride. // 3 //
The third foot here possesses the characteristic that its entire end consists of two heavy syllables (gurus), while the first foot is composed of a *manu* (eight) syllables.
This indeed is the mark (*lakṣma*) of the foot in this [meter].
If that *lavalī* plant were to become everything else as well as what is under discussion; 5.4.
That [meter] whose third quarter possesses the defining characteristic composed for the first foot, and which is joined with two heavy syllables at the end of all its quarters, is called *lavalī*.
Furthermore, in the *lavalī*, everything previously mentioned regarding the subject matter remains as before. For example:
*gaganatalamamalamalimetat* (this sky-surface is stainless and honey-filled).
Suddenly, this moon, with its mass of rays resembling flames,
produces on earth a poignant sense of instability for Lavalyā, as if she were oppressed by the transformation of worldly existence.
If the fourth [foot] first resides [in the opening],
and the final pair of syllables is heavy (guru),
while all other subsequent feet are equal [to the first], this is here called *lalitapādā*.
Therefore, this is a stream of nectar. // KVrk_5.5 //

If the first foot consists of eight syllables and the final word of the last foot occupies the position of the final foot, and all other remaining parts above are as before, with two heavy syllables (*guru*) at the end, it is called the *Amṛtadhārā* (Stream of Nectar) meter, characterized by a very graceful sequence of words. For example: [Example verse omitted per instructions]
O friend with a moon-like face, an embrace from you upon my body is like a sprinkling of sandalwood paste;
it brings delight to the pair of my ears and is exceedingly clever and heart-pleasing.
Your speech is a stream of nectar.
Piṅgalanāga, however, observes that when there is a transposition of the first quarter-verse in the *caturūrdhva* class and others, names such as *mañjarī* and so forth are applied. // 5 //
// The Section on Padacaturūrdhva //
[The Section on Udgatā (5.6–8):

In the first [foot], *saja* (sa, ja) followed by a short and a long syllable (*salaghukau*) constitutes *Udgatā*. Then, in the subsequent [feet], *na*, *sa*, *ja*, *ga*, and *ruka* (*guruka*) [constitute it].
When three *aṅghris* (feet) have reached the *bha*, *na*, *ja*, and *la* [syllables] and are joined with a *ga*, one should recite the foot as *sa*, *ja*, *sa*, *ja*, and *ga*. KVrk_5.6 //

In the first quarter (pāda), there are the *sagaṇa*, *jagaṇa*, and *sagaṇa* gaṇas followed by a short syllable (*laghu*); likewise, in the second quarter, there are the *nagaṇa*, *sagaṇa*, *jagaṇa*, and a long syllable (*guru*). The third quarter, characterized by the number three, consists of the *bhagaṇa*, *nagaṇa*, *jagaṇa*, a short syllable, and a long syllable; it is joined with these.
In the fourth foot, where there are the *sagaṇa*, *jagaṇa*, *sagaṇa*, *jagaṇa*, and a long syllable, that [meter] is named *udgatā*.
"Ekata" means that one should recite the first [verse] together with the second without delay; for example:
"Those who have conquered stinginess, the virtuous ones, who have also cast off the kinsman that is blemish..."
Upon suddenly beholding a young woman, his body—previously broad and well-developed—certainly undergoes a transformation.
If the entire *lakṣma* (the *saurabhaka* mark) occurs in three feet with the sequence of rising and falling (*udgatāgatam*),
and if in this case the *bhaga* (the *vātormī* mark) occurs in the third foot, it becomes *saurabhaka*.

If in the third foot of the *udgatā* there are the *ragaṇa*, *nagaṇa*, *bhagaṇa*, and a heavy syllable (*guru*), then it is the metre named *saurabhaka*. For example: "The Malaya breeze blows very gently from the sky toward the young women separated from their lovers, as if exhaling the fragrance of camphor. (7)
If the third foot consists of *na*, *ya*, *ga*, and a pair of *sa*s,
that is called *Lalita* by those of vast intellect, provided its remainder is indeed equal to the preceding [foot].
If, in the third foot of the *udgatā*, there are two *nagaṇas* and two *sagaṇas*, then it is named *lalitā*;
the remainder is like the *udgatā*. For example:
"The fresh grace, delightful with playful movements of the limbs, is full-fleshed."
O friend, this intoxicated woman joyfully performs an exquisite dance before you.
// The Chapter on Arising //
[The section on Upasthitapracupita (5.9–11):
In the first foot, the gaṇas are ma, sa, ja, bha, and two gas; the other three feet are distinct from that, consisting of sa, na, ja, ra, and a ga, as well as na, na, and a sa.
With three *gaṇas* of three syllables each, followed by a *jayau* (two long syllables), it is called *pracupita*; when measured as *mita-mudita*, it is known as *upasthitapūrvā*.
In its first quarter, there are the *magaṇa*, *sagaṇa*, *jagaṇa*, and *bhagaṇa*, followed by two *gurus* together;
the meaning is that the other three quarters are each distinct [from this].
In the second quarter, there are the *sagaṇa*, *nagaṇa*, *jagaṇa*, *ragaṇa*, and a *guru*; likewise, in the third quarter, there are two *nagaṇas* and a *sagaṇa*; and in the fourth [quarter]...
That meter which consists of three *nagaṇas* followed by a *jagaṇa* and a *yagaṇa* is called *upasthitapūrva*, meaning *upasthitapracupita*. For example:

"Having ascended the mango tree, beloved by cuckoos, which is radiant with blossoms and displays fresh clusters of flowers, the female bee, full of pride, proclaims the great festival of the Lord of Love through the sounds of her own sweet humming. (9)
In the third foot of nine syllables, with *sa* and *na*, joined by *na* and *sa*, and the first quarter consisting of *kṛta-ya-ti*, it is called *Vardhamāna*;
the other three quarters here are similar to the preceding one—this is indeed the metre declared by those of expansive intellect.

That same *padacaturūrdhva* becomes [the meter] *vardhamāna* when the third foot consists of two *nagaṇas* followed by a *sagaṇa* and a *nagaṇa*, provided that the pause (*yati*) is made according to the first foot of the *caturūrdhva*. That is to say, it is so called when the pause of the qualifying action is made as in the first foot. In this system, the teachers have stated that such a verse, with the other three feet similar to the preceding one, is named *vardhamāna*. For example: [Example omitted per instructions]
The *aśoka* tree, struck by the feet of women with their breasts naturally uplifted, flourishes;
even the *bakula* tree experiences an abundance of blossoming flowers when sprinkled with the wine from the mouths of beautiful young women.
If in this very third foot there should be *ta*, *ja*, and *ra*, with a pause after the first [foot], they call it Ārṣabha;
if that triad preceded by Śuddhavirāṭ is also equal to the preceding one, [it is called] Aparavaktra. (KVrk 5.11)

In this very *padacaturūrdhva* meter, if the third foot consists of a *tagaṇa*, a *jagaṇa*, and a *ragaṇa*, while the other three feet are identical to the preceding [first] one, then they call it *śuddhavirāḍārṣabha*—meaning a *śuddhavirāṭ* situated before an *ārṣabha*. For example:
*bibhrāṇā vadanam śaśāṃkabimbasamānam kamalāyatanayanā kṛśāṅgaśobhitā* [She who bears a face equal to the orb of the moon, whose eyes are like lotuses, and who is graced by her slender limbs.]
This woman, with her pair of full and lofty breasts, produces exceeding joy. // 11 //
// The Section on Upasthitapracupita //
That which has uneven syllables in its quarters, or quarters that are unequal like the ten dharmas,
and whose meter is not specified here— this is called a *gāthā* by the wise.

That [verse] in which the feet consist of unequal syllables is called *viṣamākṣarapāda*. Likewise, that which has eight, ten, seven, or nine syllables, being unequal in all its feet—whether it be three-footed or six-footed—is like the *daśadharma* [verse]. For example: "Ten do not know the Dharma; O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, learn who they are."

One who is intoxicated, one who is negligent, one who is insane, one who is exhausted, one who is angry, one who is hungry, one who is in haste, one who is fearful, one who is greedy, and one who is lustful— these are the ten [who are unfit].
Thus ends the six-footed verse (*ṣaṭpadī-gāthā*).
Whatever [metrical forms] such as these have not been explicitly mentioned in this treatise on prosody but are seen in actual usage, those are called *gāthā* by the learned.
One should understand that all [verses] beginning with *maṅgalagītikā*, *āveṣṭaka*, *vipad*, *vidhruvaka*, *cañcarī*, *pāddhatikā*, and *dvipathaka* are designated as *gāthā*.
Because the Vedic meters are infinite, it is impossible to state them individually; therefore, a single technical designation has been established to encompass them all. // 12 //
Thus ends the fifth chapter, on Irregular Meters, in the Vṛttaratnākara-chandovṛtti titled Sukavihṛdayānandinī, composed by Sulhaṇa.
The Sixth Chapter:
The Chapter on the Six Conditions [The Arrangement]

The expansion (prastāra), the lost (naṣṭa), the indicated (uddiṣṭa), the operation with one, two, and so forth (laghugurukriyā), the number (saṃkhyā), and the application of the path (adhvayoga)— these six are known as the secondary applications (pratyaya).

Now he states the six conditions for the meters (vṛtta) already mentioned: "Having placed a light syllable beneath the first heavy syllable in the line, and having done so for each subsequent heavy syllable, one should repeatedly apply this same procedure to the remainder. (KVrk 6.2)
In this manner, one should add long syllables to the deficient positions until all are short;
this is declared as the *prastāra* by those who know the science of prosody (*chandovicitivedibhiḥ*).
When the first foot consists entirely of heavy syllables, as many heavy syllables as there are syllables in a foot of the meter are written down.
For example,

in a four-syllable meter, having placed (i.e., set down) a light syllable in the lower section beneath the first heavy syllable, then, from that placed light syllable, [one proceeds] downward from the remaining syllables...
He asks, "What is established?
and says: "As above, so below; as the rest.
If above it is heavy, then below it is also heavy; if above it is light, then below it is also light—the rest is the same.
The meaning is that an equal [number] is placed above. By that, three heavy syllables (guru) are established immediately after the light one (laghu).
"Again, one should perform this procedure once more."
Having placed a short syllable beneath a long one, one should arrange the remainder as above; thus one should perform this procedure again.

When there is a long syllable above, because the rule "having placed a short syllable beneath the long one" no longer applies, the meaning is that the deficient space is filled with long syllables, according to the rule: "one should give [the remaining] long syllables in the deficient positions.
In this manner, the placement should be performed until the entire *pāda* consists of short syllables.
It is called *prastāra* because it is spread out; it is a specific arrangement of syllables.
Thus, in a four-syllable foot, there are sixteen meters (*vṛtta*). It is called *chandoviciti* because the meters are analyzed within it; it is the science of prosody (*chandaḥśāstra*).
The *prastāra* has been explained. // 2-3 //
[The "lost" (naṣṭa)]:
Now he speaks in order to explain the "lost" [method]:
"Whatever be the number of the lost [verse], when that is halved and halved again, if it is even, there is a long syllable (la)."
Having placed one [syllable] on the uneven [positions], there shall be a long syllable at each successive half of that.

Among the meters shown in the *prastāra*, when a particular meter has been lost or omitted, one should take the numerical value—starting from one—of that lost meter; if that number is even, halve it repeatedly, and at each stage where the number is even, there will be a short (*la*) syllable.
If the number is odd, add one, and then halve it repeatedly; at each stage, there will be a long (*ga*) syllable.
Just as in this four-syllable meter the fifth permutation is lost;
its numerical value is five, and it does not yield a half.
When one is added to it, then there are six.
They are divided by half;
thus there are three and a half.
When that is halved again, the teacher is reached; yet they do not give another half.
There are four *saikas*;
these also constitute half [of a *dvaṇḍa*], and when that half is further divided, it is equal to two *gurus*.
When that half is further divided, a *laghu* is obtained; furthermore, one does not grant half of that.
One should add one to that and again obtain the teacher (the divisor) as half of that;
such is the example for the "lost" [number].
And likewise:
The first two are heavy (guru), followed by a light (laghu) syllable after them, and then a heavy syllable;
this is the fifth metre (*vṛtta*) in the four-syllable *chandas*. // 4 //
[The section] "Recited" (*uddiṣṭam*):
he speaks in order to explain what has been recited.
Regarding the "recited," he says: "One should write the numbers from one upward, doubling each preceding one."
But those figures which are small in that [array], when combined with their respective successors, shall become [the result].
Someone asked: "Which of those meters is the *prastāryaka*? In response to this inquiry regarding the knowledge of numbers, that which was indicated is now stated.
In the previous case, the meter was not known;
therefore, it is recovered by means of its numerical value.

Furthermore, in this case, the metrical pattern (vṛtta) is known, but the number [of syllables] is not known; therefore, for the sake of fully understanding that number, this "indicated" (uddiṣṭa) method is stated.
Starting from the first syllable of that indicated meter, one should write numbers above them that double successively, as follows:

In this very four-syllable meter (*caturakṣara-chandas*), one *vṛtta* (verse-pattern) is pointed out (*uddiṣṭa*): its two syllables are heavy (*guru*), then a light (*laghu*), and then again a heavy. In that pointed-out *vṛtta*, those which stand upon the light syllable are called "light-positions" (*laghusthā*). Furthermore, by those four numbers together with one—making five—one arrives at the "pointed-out" (*uddiṣṭa*);
it becomes the "pointed-out count" (*uddiṣṭasaṃkhyā*).
The meaning is that in a four-syllable meter, that fifth [type] becomes the *vṛtta*. // 5 //
[The procedure for one, two, and so forth, laghus]: He states [the following] for the purpose of the operation of one, two, and so forth, laghus:
"The syllables occurring in the meter, increased by one, are arranged from top to bottom."
And one should place these one by one in ascending order, from the first onwards.
One should turn back from the penultimate syllable, omitting one [syllable] at a time from above;
starting from the first syllable of the guru, in this manner, the operation of one, two, and so forth, applies to the heavy syllables.
As many as there are syllables in the metrical foot, so many are those [dots], increased by one.
For example, in the four-syllable class, there are four syllables; these, increased by one, become five.
One should place these, situated in an ascending order—that is, positioned one above the other—in the sequence beginning with one, depositing them higher and higher.
From the penultimate—that is, from the position adjacent to the last—it would turn back and emerge;
abandoning and avoiding each one from the upper portion.
To the question, "In what manner does this operation of adding one, two, and so forth proceed? he says:
Regarding the phrase "from the first guru above," this means from the first heavy syllable situated above.
What is the meaning?
It means from the side of a metrical foot consisting entirely of heavy syllables.
It is said that the first meter is conceived as having a single syllable entirely heavy (guru).
This is demonstrated in the *prastāra* [diagram] by the rule:

"In a foot consisting entirely of heavy syllables, one should place a light (laghu) syllable after the first. Therefore, from that [initial state], this process of introducing one, two, and so on, light syllables proceeds below it.
In that regard, when five colors are arranged in an upper-lower relationship, one situated below is placed upon those above it.

That [lower one] remains exactly as it was, because by virtue of the repetition "discarding one by one from above," the placement occurs all at once without remaining stationary; since there is no further act of placing, the discarding of each one individually is not possible, and therefore it remains in its own essential nature.
In this way, it is cast upward;
then, in the second position, there are two syllables, which are added to the third, making three;
and that is placed in the fourth, making four.

"It ceases from the penultimate [place], discarding one by one from above. This means that the single [unit] at the top is discarded and not added there. The repetition (*vīpsā*) indicates that the action of depositing proceeds again from the lower part; thus, the very one situated below is deposited in the second place, making three there.
That [total] is then deposited in the third, making six there. Discarding the one at the top, it ceases.
The first *vṛtta* consists of a single [syllable] entirely heavy (*sarvaguru*). From that, the operations of one, two, and so forth light syllables proceed.
Thus, there is one entirely heavy, four with two light syllables, six with three light syllables, four with four light syllables, and one entirely light (*sarvalaghu*).
This operation of light syllables is understood through the expansion (*prastāra*) of all-light syllables; this same sequence applies even for *vṛttas* of five syllables and beyond. (6–7)
[Example: 1 41 631 4321 11111] [Calculation] He states this for the purpose of enumeration.
[The sum of the digits in the light operation (lagukriyā), when mixed with the number, or that same sum plus one, shall produce this. In the light operation,
the collection of those digits— when mixed, that is, compressed together— becomes the number.
This, first of all, constitutes the retention (*dhāraṇa*).

Likewise, one, four, six, and four—these, when added together, indeed become sixteen; the meaning is that when the class of four-syllable meters is being expanded (*prastāryamāṇāyām*), there are sixteen meters.
And that expansion has already been explained previously.

He states another alternative: "The sum—that is, the unification—of those doubled numbers which are above the stated verse, or that [sum] plus one, shall produce—that is, generate—this number. For example:
In the four-syllable class, the numbers placed above are doubled; their sum is fifteen, which, with one added, is sixteen. // 8 //
[The Application of the Paths] Regarding the meaning of the paths, he says:
"The number itself, doubled and diminished by one, is proclaimed by the wise as the path."
One should make the extent of the circle one finger-breadth below, and likewise one finger-breadth [above].

In the class of four-syllable meters, that which is the number sixteen, doubled, becomes thirty-two; when one is subtracted from it, it is thirty-one. This is proclaimed as the "path" (adhvan) by the wise.
How so?
It should effect a pervasion of the verse-measure equal to the length of a finger (aṅgulikī). // 9 //
Now, once again, the poet describes himself along with his father, following the order of succession:

"In the lineage of Kaśyapa was born a Brahmin named Pavyeka, whose multitude of virtues was manifest, who was a knower of the Śaiva Siddhānta, and whose intellect was exceedingly pure in the realization of the principles of Śiva. (KVrk 6.10)
His son was Kedāra, whose mind was one-pointedly devoted solely to the worship of the pair of Śiva’s feet;
by him this delightful work, titled *Vṛttaratnākara*, was composed.

He was born in the lineage (*vaṃśa*) or family (*anvaya*) of Kaśyapa. Although the word *kaśyapa*—derived from "one who drinks the *kaśya*, i.e., the *soma*"—is used here to denote liquor (*surā*), it nevertheless refers to the *soma* in this context, because drinking liquor is forbidden for a Brahmin or twice-born (*dvija*). By the sense of "lineage" or "family," his status as a follower of that tradition is expressed.
He is a knower of those established doctrines (*siddhāntas*) which belong to Śiva; these are the Śaiva [doctrines].
This is a form of the root *vid* meaning "to investigate" (*vicāraṇe*), and not of *vid* meaning "to know" (*jñāne*),
because the latter is impossible in this context.

For he who investigates and reflects necessarily knows; indeed, one cannot investigate what is unknown. Such a person especially fulfills [the goals of] heaven, liberation, and so forth—he is a *vipra* (brāhmaṇa), one whose intellect (*mati*) is exceedingly pure (*vimalatara*).
"Pure" means his intellect is stainless, expansive, agile, and captivating; thus, he is one of preeminent purity of mind.
Where?
In the understanding of the Śaiva scriptures.
He was one whose mind was single-pointed and fixed upon the propitiation of that specific deity named Śiva—the peaceful one known as Kedāra—who was his son.
Likewise, by that Kedāra, a delightful, charming, and captivating meter was composed with great excellence, known by the name Vṛttaratnākara. // 10-11 //
Thus ends the sixth chapter, concerning the six suffixes, in the *Chandovṛtti* titled *Sukavihṛdayānandinī*, composed by the scholar Śrī Sulhaṇa.
